These decompose `dispatchToolCallImpl` (the approval/policy/spine pipeline every tool call goes through; the security heart of the agent) into `cli/src/core/tool_pipeline.ts`-style stages and moved the complexity baseline. They merged without an independent review by me: review them now. Base for comparison: release commit `09eb0b12f` (merge of #811, before slice 3: check `git log --first-parent` and use the commit just before #817 merged). Read first: the plan `/home/mike/nexus-wt/_plans/PF_SB_MT_PA_PLAN.md` section "MT-2" (design, security analysis: "no phase changes order; refusal receipts keep exact text and status; the baseline moves tighten-only, once, with owner acknowledgement"), `docs/TOOL_REGISTRY.md`, the PR diffs and PR bodies/comments (`gh pr view 817 818 819 820 --comments`), and my review of #804. The slice-1 characterization (`cli/test/tool_surface_characterization.test.ts`, `tool_dispatch_characterization.test.ts`, fixtures `model_tools_v1.json`, `tool_bindings_v1.json`) MUST still pass with the fixtures UNEDITED: check `git diff 09eb0b12f..origin/release/v1.3.0 -- cli/test/fixtures cli/test/helpers/tool_characterization.ts cli/test/tool_*characterization*` and justify every change.
Judge: (1) Differential behaviour at base vs tip for the dispatch pipeline: build a harness (second detached worktree for base) that runs the SAME scripted calls through `dispatchToolCall` at both and compares status, error text, receipts (stable fields), journal/flight events order, approvals asked (order and content), and tool execution counts: cover EVERY registered tool in each approval posture (the slice-1 table), unknown tool, null/ill-typed arguments (the characterization pinned a TypeError on JSON null: did any slice change it? if so is it intended), delegated allow-list, role allow/deny, skill constraints, checkpoint read-only fallback, managed policy forbid/require-human/`clampAlwaysApproval`, egress allowlist, verification-edit decision, CS-9 command rules, injection ask, ask decision, skill confirm, needs-input/confirm, plugin notify, journal/baseline capture, spine execute, after-hooks (eval receipts, journal end, `notifyToolResult`, `run_tests` attempts, file/diff tracking, VR-3 events, flight), hooks (HK-1 contextAdmission/evidenceEmission stage ordering: `hooks_gate_bypass`), P10 budgets, and the subagent path (`runSubagent` calls dispatch). Any difference in ORDER of gates, in what is approved/denied, or in a receipt's text/status/code is a finding. (2) Security properties: no gate skipped on any path (try to find a call path that reaches `spine.execute` without passing every gate that base applied: grep the new stage functions for early returns; verify each stage's refusal still short-circuits subsequent stages; verify exceptions in a stage are handled as base did (fail closed)); `this: any` binding losses; shared mutable state between stages. (3) Complexity baseline move (#820): the five critical functions' numbers before/after (run `cli/scripts/check_critical_complexity.ts` at base and tip), what exactly changed in `critical-complexity-baseline.json` (revision, functions list added/removed), `critical_complexity.test.ts` updates; is the move tighten-only (every tracked function's CC/nesting at or below its OLD baseline, new functions tracked)? (4) Registry: `capabilities()` bypass (register/unregister/setHandler on the underlying CapabilityRegistry) closed or still open (my #804 follow-ups: `baselineTools` mutable export; `native` binding handler precedence)? (5) Docs claims (`TOOL_REGISTRY.md`, CHANGELOG).
Run at the tip, one at a time: the slice-1 files, `tool_registry`, `critical_complexity`, `capabilities`, `lsp_shape`, `tool_groups`, `role_deny_lists`, `acp_mapping`, `tool_grammar*`, `command_rules_dispatch`, `managed_policy_dispatch`, `vllm_nullable_dispatch`, `approval_policy`, `injection_gate`, `security_gates`, `sandbox_denial_events` (TMPDIR=/dev/shm), `agt111_subagent_parity`, `mcp_tool_through_spine`, `hooks_*`, `subagent_delegation_authority`, `spine*`, `sidecar`, `acp_stdio`, `protocol_parity`, and `context_convergence` (very slow: run once with `timeout 900`); failing sets at base vs tip must be equal; `cd cli && npx tsc --noEmit -p .`; the complexity gate (exit code); `node scripts/check_invariants.mjs`. Mutations (copy aside, restore from the copy, never `git checkout`): swap two adjacent gate stages in the new pipeline; make one stage's refusal fall through; skip the managed-policy stage: each must fail a test (say which, or say none: a gate-ordering mutation that no test catches is a finding).
Rules: do NOT edit ~/nexus-code (it has someone else's uncommitted `cli/src/agent.ts` edit: ignore it, do not use that checkout) or existing worktrees. Two detached worktrees: `git -C ~/nexus-code fetch origin && git -C ~/nexus-code worktree add --detach ~/nexus-wt/revmt2 origin/release/v1.3.0` and `... ~/nexus-wt/revmt2-base 09eb0b12f` (or the commit just before #817); in each: `cp -a ~/nexus-code/cli/node_modules <wt>/cli/` and `mkdir -p <wt>/core/target/release && cp ~/nexus-wt/ls1b/core/target/release/{harness-core,nexus-tui} <wt>/core/target/release/`. Tests: `cd <wt>/cli && TMPDIR=/dev/shm HOME=$(mktemp -d) node --import tsx --test test/<name>.test.ts 2>&1 | tail -20`. Never touch the real ~/.nexus, ~/.config/nexus, /etc/nexus; no network; no live inference. Stop processes by their own pid; never `pkill -f`; never delete outside your own temp dirs. No commits, pushes or GitHub comments. Remove probes and both worktrees at the end. Shell is zsh (`bash -c` for loops); prefix `rtk proxy` if output looks filtered; a safety check blocks scripts containing `rm`.
Report under 600 words: verdict (BEHAVIOUR PRESERVED / PRESERVED WITH FOLLOW-UPS / DIFFERENCES FOUND) on the merged code at the exact tip SHA; the differential result (number of scenarios, any difference with the exact scenario); gate-order findings; the complexity baseline before/after table and whether the move is tighten-only; owner acknowledgement present or not; registry follow-ups status; failing sets base vs tip; mutation results; what you did not check.

## Workflow

### Plan
- Plan any non-trivial task (3+ steps or an architectural decision) before building: write the plan to `tasks/todo.md` as checkable items and check in before implementing. Plan the verification steps too.
- When something goes sideways, stop and re-plan at once.
- Tick items off as you go, give a high-level summary of each change, and end with a review section in `tasks/todo.md`.

### Subagents
- Keep the main context clean: offload research, exploration and parallel analysis to subagents, one tack per subagent. Throw more subagents at a complex problem.

### Lessons
- After any user correction, add the pattern to `tasks/lessons.md` as a rule that prevents the same mistake, and iterate until the mistake rate drops. Review the file at session start.

### Done means proven
- A task is complete when evidence shows it works: tests run, logs checked, behaviour diffed against main where relevant. Ask: would a staff engineer approve this?

### Elegance
- For a non-trivial change, pause and look for a more elegant way; when a fix feels hacky, implement the elegant solution with everything you now know. Keep simple, obvious fixes simple. Challenge your own work before presenting it.

### Bug reports
- Fix them from the evidence: logs, errors, failing tests, CI failures included. Resolve without being walked through it.

## Principles
- **Simplicity first**: the smallest change that works, touching only what is necessary.
- **Root cause**: no temporary fixes; senior-developer standard.

@RTK.md

# graphify
`/graphify` → invoke the Skill tool with `skill: "graphify"` (`~/.claude/skills/graphify/SKILL.md`) before anything else.

# RTK (Rust Token Killer)

A hook rewrites shell commands through `rtk` (60-90% fewer tokens): write ordinary commands (`git status` runs as `rtk git status`).

- Raw output: `rtk proxy <cmd>`. Use it to debug, and whenever a rewritten `grep`, `awk` or `sed` pipeline returns filtered or odd output; rerun it raw before trusting it.
- Savings: `rtk gain`, `rtk gain --history`. Missed opportunities: `rtk discover`.
- If `rtk gain` fails, a different `rtk` is installed (reachingforthejack/rtk, Rust Type Kit); check `which rtk`.

## Principles

1. Don't assume. Don't hide confusion. Surface tradeoffs.
2. Minimum code that solves the problem. Nothing speculative.
3. Touch only what you must. Clean up only your mess.
4. Define success criteria. Loop until verified.

## Agent workflow

Specialised agents live in `~/.claude/agents/` (their descriptions are in the agent list). Delegate any feature, bug fix or significant change to **`@orchestrator`**: it runs the pipeline and returns one structured summary (changes, test results, review findings, issues) while the verbose output stays in its context.

Pipeline: `@architect` plans and identifies affected files → `@coder` writes code (linter only, no tests) → `@tester` writes and runs tests, looping with coder on failures → `@reviewer` reviews the final diff (security, performance, readability, consistency) → `@design-qa` screenshots affected pages at mobile, tablet and desktop (UI changes only).

Call a single agent directly for one stage: architect, coder, tester, reviewer, design-qa, security-auditor, migration-planner (alembic, sqlite3), api-designer, ci-validator (GitLab CI).

Handle these yourself, without delegating: codebase questions, reading and explaining code, git operations, deployments, config changes.

Affected tests across all sub-projects (Go, Playwright, pytest): `./scripts/verify.sh` (the tester agent uses it).

## Browsing

Use the gstack `/browse` skill for all web browsing, and keep `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*` tools out of use.

## Sub-projects

| Project | Stack | Location |
|---------|-------|----------|
| SyndicateCode | Go 1.25, bubbletea TUI, gRPC, sqlite3 | `./SyndicateCode/` |
| aisyndicate | Next.js 16, React, TypeScript, Radix UI | `./aisyndicate/` |
| syndicateclaw | Python 3.12, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, alembic | `./syndicateclaw/` |
| controlplane-enterprise | Go, enterprise control plane | `./controlplane-enterprise/` |
| syndicategate | Go, backend service | `./syndicategate/` |

## graphify

`graphify-out/` holds a knowledge graph (god nodes, communities, cross-file relationships).

- For a codebase question, start with `graphify query "<question>"` when `graphify-out/graph.json` exists; use `graphify path "<A>" "<B>"` for relationships and `graphify explain "<concept>"` for one concept. Each returns a scoped subgraph, usually far smaller than `GRAPH_REPORT.md` or raw grep.
- Navigate broadly through `graphify-out/wiki/index.md` when it exists.
- Read `graphify-out/GRAPH_REPORT.md` for broad architecture review, or when query, path and explain fall short.
- After modifying code, run `graphify update .` (AST-only, no API cost).

# nexus-code agent guide

TypeScript CLI (`cli/`), Rust core (`core/`), eval harness (`eval/`). Current plans: `docs/v1.2.1/PLAN.md`, then `docs/v1.3.0/PLAN.md`. Per-release records live in `docs/releases/` and `docs/evidence/`.

## Build and test
- Build: `make build` (core, then `tsc` in `cli/`). Everything: `make test`; the CI-equivalent run: `make test-ci`. Lint the core with `cargo clippy`; `cli/` has no lint script, `npm --prefix cli run build` type-checks it.
- One TypeScript test file: `cd cli && HOME=$(mktemp -d) node --import tsx --test test/<name>.test.ts`. A throwaway `HOME` is mandatory: a test that touched the real `HOME` once overwrote `~/.config/nexus/config.env`.
- Done = the affected test files pass, plus `tsc` for TypeScript changes. CI is the arbiter; a failure that appears only locally comes from host state first (an unbuilt `cli/dist` or Rust core, a stray `/tmp/.git`), so rule that out before calling it a defect.
- Test-runner or process-handling changes run on Node 22 and 24: the two emit different `node:test` events.
- Rust builds use an isolated `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` per worktree.
- Preserve existing comments and unrelated changes.
- Entire CLI: export `ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE=file` before any `entire` command. The Entire gate no longer counts toward merging.

## Reference coding with XERJ (required)
- Before writing non-trivial code that has a peer-project analogue (feature, protocol, parser, worktree or provider handling, tool, test harness), read what mature projects do: query the local XERJ node, then record what you took, borrowed or rejected in the PR's "Reference coding" section. Exempt: trivial edits, doc-only changes, fixes fully specified by a failing test.
- Node, commands, corpora, licence and privacy rules, the field report, and the fallback when XERJ is unavailable ("XERJ unavailable: <reason>" plus `git grep`): `docs/XERJ_REFERENCE_CODING.md`. Read it when you start that first query.

## Concurrency, claims and release authority
- Several agents can work here: follow `docs/v1.0.0/CONCURRENCY.md`. Claim a slice or hot file under `$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/nexus-claims/` before editing; one worktree and branch per slice (`~/nexus-wt/`), never `~/nexus-code` itself; isolate `HOME` for every test or probe; stop a process by its own pid, never `pkill -f`; check `git log` for foreign commits before each commit.
- Take the `GATEWAY` claim for any inference run; the key comes from the environment (`~/.config/nexus/config.env`) and is never printed. The gateway is the only live provider.
- Push, tag and publish only on an explicit owner instruction; release authority is the owner's.

## Merging and releasing
Bias to correct: a green PR is not a green `main`, and a pushed tag cannot be taken back.
- When merging: required checks are `test-matrix (22)`, `test-matrix (24)`, `linux-x86_64`; read each check's conclusion (empty or in-progress is not success). Merge with a merge commit, `gh pr merge <n> --merge --match-head-commit <full-sha>`. PRs that touch one subsystem merge one at a time, each followed by the CI run on `main`: two PRs green alone can break `main` together.
- When a PR's checks look wrong after `main` moved: PR checks run on GitHub's merge commit, so confirm the run checked out the current `merge_commit_sha` (`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/pulls/<n> --jq .merge_commit_sha`); a stale one tests old content.
- When cutting a stable release: make a version-only commit directly on the accepted RC (`node scripts/check-version-only-diff.mjs <rc-ref> <stable-ref>`), land it on `main` through a merge-commit PR, and only then tag, because `release.yml` requires the tagged commit to be an ancestor of `main`. Version tags are immutable: re-run a failed run, or move to the next RC or patch. Then follow `docs/RELEASE_PROCESS.md`.
- When reporting a gate or a result: state it as measured ("ledger closed, qualification pending"), record failed runs unaltered, and make no frontier-grade claim without external qualification.
- Before tagging or merging, check: required checks green at the exact head? CI on `main` green after the previous merge? Tagged commit an ancestor of `main`? Claims match the evidence?

Delegate any feature, bug fix or significant change to **`@orchestrator`**: it runs the pipeline and returns one structured summary (changes, test results, review findings, issues) while the verbose output stays in its context.

Pipeline: `@architect` plans and identifies affected files → `@coder` writes code (linter only, no tests) → `@tester` writes and runs tests, looping with coder on failures → `@reviewer` reviews the final diff (security, performance, readability, consistency) → `@design-qa` screenshots affected pages at mobile, tablet and desktop (UI changes only).

Call a single agent directly for one stage: architect, coder, tester, reviewer, design-qa, security-auditor, migration-planner (alembic, sqlite3), api-designer, ci-validator (GitLab CI).

Handle these yourself, without delegating: codebase questions, reading and explaining code, git operations, deployments, config changes.

Bias to correct: a green PR is not a green `main`, and a pushed tag cannot be taken back.

## Review Priorities (in order)

1. **Security** — vulnerabilities, injection, auth issues, data exposure, SSRF, insecure defaults

3. **Readability** — clear naming, simple logic, easy to follow without comments
4. **Consistency** — follows existing patterns, naming conventions, project style

- **syndicateclaw** — Python 3.12, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy async, Pydantic. Full type hints. Alembic for migrations.
- **CI**: GitLab CI pipelines

## CodeGraph — Impact Analysis

Before reviewing, understand the blast radius:

```bash
git diff --name-only HEAD | codegraph affected --stdin --quiet
```

Use:
- `codegraph_impact` — what's affected by changing a symbol
- `codegraph_callers` — find every caller of a changed function
- `codegraph_context` — understand the full context around changed code

## Your Process

1. Run `git diff HEAD` or `git diff --name-only HEAD` to see what changed
2. Use codegraph to identify all affected files (including transitive)
3. Read each changed file in context
4. Check against the four priorities above
5. Verify tests were updated for affected code
6. Check architectural layer boundaries weren't violated (clean architecture)
7. Confirm Conventional Commit format is used

## Go-Specific Anti-patterns

- Naked returns in long functions
- Ignoring errors (`_ = err`)
- Mutex copied by value
- Context not propagated through call chain
- SQL queries without parameterization
- Missing `CGO_ENABLED=1` in Go build scripts for SyndicateCode

## TypeScript/Next.js Anti-patterns

- `any` type usage
- `useEffect` without proper dependency arrays
- Missing React key props in lists

Every finding must have a concrete fix — "this could be better" is not useful.

tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.

- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

- For a non-trivial change, pause and look for a more elegant way; when a fix feels hacky, implement the elegant solution with everything you now know. Keep simple, obvious fixes simple. Challenge your own work before presenting it.

# nexus-code agent guide

TypeScript CLI (`cli/`), Rust core (`core/`), eval harness (`eval/`). Current plans: `docs/v1.2.1/PLAN.md`, then `docs/v1.3.0/PLAN.md`. Per-release records live in `docs/releases/` and `docs/evidence/`.

## Build and test
- Build: `make build` (core, then `tsc` in `cli/`). Everything: `make test`; the CI-equivalent run: `make test-ci`. Lint the core with `cargo clippy`; `cli/` has no lint script, `npm --prefix cli run build` type-checks it.
- One TypeScript test file: `cd cli && HOME=$(mktemp -d) node --import tsx --test test/<name>.test.ts`. A throwaway `HOME` is mandatory: a test that touched the real `HOME` once overwrote `~/.config/nexus/config.env`.
- Done = the affected test files pass, plus `tsc` for TypeScript changes. CI is the arbiter; a failure that appears only locally comes from host state first (an unbuilt `cli/dist` or Rust core, a stray `/tmp/.git`), so rule that out before calling it a defect.
- Test-runner or process-handling changes run on Node 22 and 24: the two emit different `node:test` events.
- Rust builds use an isolated `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` per worktree.
- Preserve existing comments and unrelated changes.
- Entire CLI: export `ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE=file` before any `entire` command. The Entire gate no longer counts toward merging.

## Reference coding with XERJ (required)
- Before writing non-trivial code that has a peer-project analogue (feature, protocol, parser, worktree or provider handling, tool, test harness), read what mature projects do: query the local XERJ node, then record what you took, borrowed or rejected in the PR's "Reference coding" section. Exempt: trivial edits, doc-only changes, fixes fully specified by a failing test.
- Node, commands, corpora, licence and privacy rules, the field report, and the fallback when XERJ is unavailable ("XERJ unavailable: <reason>" plus `git grep`): `docs/XERJ_REFERENCE_CODING.md`. Read it when you start that first query.

## Concurrency, claims and release authority
- Several agents can work here: follow `docs/v1.0.0/CONCURRENCY.md`. Claim a slice or hot file under `$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/nexus-claims/` before editing; one worktree and branch per slice (`~/nexus-wt/`), never `~/nexus-code` itself; isolate `HOME` for every test or probe; stop a process by its own pid, never `pkill -f`; check `git log` for foreign commits before each commit.
- Take the `GATEWAY` claim for any inference run; the key comes from the environment (`~/.config/nexus/config.env`) and is never printed. The gateway is the only live provider.
- Push, tag and publish only on an explicit owner instruction; release authority is the owner's.

## Merging and releasing
Bias to correct: a green PR is not a green `main`, and a pushed tag cannot be taken back.
- When merging: required checks are `test-matrix (22)`, `test-matrix (24)`, `linux-x86_64`; read each check's conclusion (empty or in-progress is not success). Merge with a merge commit, `gh pr merge <n> --merge --match-head-commit <full-sha>`. PRs that touch one subsystem merge one at a time, each followed by the CI run on `main`: two PRs green alone can break `main` together.
- When a PR's checks look wrong after `main` moved: PR checks run on GitHub's merge commit, so confirm the run checked out the current `merge_commit_sha` (`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/pulls/<n> --jq .merge_commit_sha`); a stale one tests old content.
- When cutting a stable release: make a version-only commit directly on the accepted RC (`node scripts/check-version-only-diff.mjs <rc-ref> <stable-ref>`), land it on `main` through a merge-commit PR, and only then tag, because `release.yml` requires the tagged commit to be an ancestor of `main`. Version tags are immutable: re-run a failed run, or move to the next RC or patch. Then follow `docs/RELEASE_PROCESS.md`.
- When reporting a gate or a result: state it as measured ("ledger closed, qualification pending"), record failed runs unaltered, and make no frontier-grade claim without external qualification.
- Before tagging or merging, check: required checks green at the exact head? CI on `main` green after the previous merge? Tagged commit an ancestor of `main`? Claims match the evidence?

- **SyndicateCode** — Go 1.25, clean architecture (`internal/domain`, `internal/application`, `internal/infrastructure`). Error wrapping with `%w`. CGO_ENABLED=1. Conventional Commits + `[l3d.X.Y]` bead tags.
- **aisyndicate** — Next.js 14, TypeScript strict, Radix UI, React functional components. No `any`. Clean layer separation.
- **syndicateclaw** — Python 3.12, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy async, Pydantic. Full type hints. Alembic for migrations.
- **CI**: GitLab CI pipelines

## CodeGraph — Impact Analysis

Before reviewing, understand the blast radius:

```bash
git diff --name-only HEAD | codegraph affected --stdin --quiet
```

Use:
- `codegraph_impact` — what's affected by changing a symbol
- `codegraph_callers` — find every caller of a changed function
- `codegraph_context` — understand the full context around changed code

## Your Process

1. Run `git diff HEAD` or `git diff --name-only HEAD` to see what changed
2. Use codegraph to identify all affected files (including transitive)
3. Read each changed file in context
4. Check against the four priorities above
5. Verify tests were updated for affected code
6. Check architectural layer boundaries weren't violated (clean architecture)
7. Confirm Conventional Commit format is used

## Go-Specific Anti-patterns

- Naked returns in long functions
- Ignoring errors (`_ = err`)
- Mutex copied by value
- Context not propagated through call chain
- SQL queries without parameterization
- Missing `CGO_ENABLED=1` in Go build scripts for SyndicateCode

## TypeScript/Next.js Anti-patterns

- `any` type usage
- `useEffect` without proper dependency arrays
- Missing React key props in lists
- Direct DOM manipulation instead of React state
- Unhandled promise rejections
- Sensitive data in client-side state or URLs

## Python/FastAPI Anti-patterns

- Sync blocking calls in async routes
- Missing Pydantic validation
- Raw SQL without parameterization
- Missing alembic migration for schema changes
- Broad `except Exception` without proper handling

## Findings Format

Every finding must have a concrete fix — "this could be better" is not useful.

## Response Format

```
### Blockers
- `file:line` — issue → fix

### Suggestions
- `file:line` — issue → fix

### Good
- [What was done well — reinforce patterns worth keeping]
```

If no blockers: say "No blockers found."

You have a persistent, file-based memory system at `/home/mike/nexus-code/.claude/agent-memory/reviewer/`. This directory already exists — write to it directly with the Write tool (do not run mkdir or check for its existence).

## What NOT to save in memory

- Code patterns, conventions, architecture, file paths, or project structure — these can be derived by reading the current project state.
- Git history, recent changes, or who-changed-what — `git log` / `git blame` are authoritative.
- Debugging solutions or fix recipes — the fix is in the code; the commit message has the context.
- Anything already documented in CLAUDE.md files.
- Ephemeral task details: in-progress work, temporary state, current conversation context.

## How to save memories

Saving a memory is a two-step process:

**Step 1** — write the memory to its own file (e.g., `user_role.md`, `feedback_testing.md`) using this frontmatter format:

```markdown
---
name: {{short-kebab-case-slug}}
description: {{one-line summary, used to decide relevance in future conversations, so be specific}}
metadata:
  type: {{user, feedback, project, reference}}
---

{{memory content — for feedback/project types, structure as: rule/fact, then **Why:** and **How to apply:** lines. Link related memories with [[their-name]].}}
```

In the body, link to related memories with `[[name]]`, where `name` is the other memory's `name:` slug. Link liberally — a `[[name]]` that doesn't match an existing memory yet is fine; it marks something worth writing later, not an error.

**Step 2** — add a pointer to that file in `MEMORY.md`. `MEMORY.md` is an index, not a memory — each entry should be one line, under ~150 characters: `- [Title](file.md) — one-line hook`. It has no frontmatter. Never write memory content directly into `MEMORY.md`.

- `MEMORY.md` is always loaded into your conversation context — lines after 200 will be truncated, so keep the index concise
- Keep the name, description, and type fields in memory files up-to-date with the content
- Organize memory semantically by topic, not chronologically
- Update or remove memories that turn out to be wrong or outdated

- When memories seem relevant, or the user references prior-conversation work.
- You MUST access memory when the user explicitly asks you to check, recall, or remember.
- If the user says to *ignore* or *not use* memory: Do not apply remembered facts, cite, compare against, or mention memory content.
- Memory records can become stale over time. Use memory as context for what was true at a given point in time. Before answering the user or building assumptions based solely on information in memory records, verify that the memory is still correct and up-to-date by reading the current state of the files or resources. If a recalled memory conflicts with current information, trust what you observe now — and update or remove the stale memory rather than acting on it.

## Before recommending from memory

A memory that names a specific function, file, or flag is a claim that it existed *when the memory was written*. It may have been renamed, removed, or never merged. Before recommending it:

- If the memory names a file path: check the file exists.
- If the memory names a function or flag: grep for it.
- If the user is about to act on your recommendation (not just asking about history), verify first.

"The memory says X exists" is not the same as "X exists now."

A memory that summarizes repo state (activity logs, architecture snapshots) is frozen in time. If the user asks about *recent* or *current* state, prefer `git log` or reading the code over recalling the snapshot.

## Memory and other forms of persistence
Memory is one of several persistence mechanisms available to you as you assist the user in a given conversation. The distinction is often that memory can be recalled in future conversations and should not be used for persisting information that is only useful within the scope of the current conversation.

- `tool_groups.test.ts`, `role_deny_lists.test.ts`, `acp_mapping.test.ts`, `tool_grammar*.test.ts`, `context_convergence.test.ts`
    (claimed);
  - dispatch: `command_rules_dispatch`, `managed_policy_dispatch`, `vllm_nullable_dispatch`, `approval_policy`, `injection_gate`,
    `security_gates`, `sandbox_denial_events`, `subagent_delegation_authority` (claimed), `agt111_subagent_parity`;
  - G-3 spread across `acp_stdio.test.ts:182,221`, `sidecar.test.ts:232-351`, `verify_hostile.test.ts` (claimed),
    `managed_policy_*`, `repl_approval_e2e`.
  - **No test snapshots the full model-visible list per context, and none snapshots the handler resolution per tool.** Those come first.

### Design
- **`cli/src/core/tool_registry.ts` (new):**
  ```ts
  export type ToolBinding =
    | { kind: "native"; handler: CapabilityHandler }   // today's spine.registerHandler tools
    | { kind: "bridge" }                                // RustCoreBridge.executeTool (today's registerBridgeCapabilities set)
    | { kind: "extension" };                            // MCP / plugin via the plugin pipeline (today's defaultHandler)
  export type OfferRule = "always" | "group" | "skills" | "objective" | "requirements" | "mask" | "until-all-groups";
  export interface RegisteredTool { spec: CanonicalCapability; binding: ToolBinding; offer: OfferRule }
  export class ToolRegistry {
    register(t: RegisteredTool): void;      // throws: duplicate name; spec.handler set (one source only); extension effect not exec|egress; non-extension without binding
    resolve(name: string): RegisteredTool | undefined;
    modelTools(ctx: OfferContext): ToolDefinition[];  // exactly today's effectiveTools order and filters
    capabilities(): CapabilityRegistry;     // adapter: existing getByToolName callers keep working
  }
  ```
  The order is the insertion order of today's `effectiveTools` array: `HARNESS_TOOLS` order, then `ENABLE_TOOLS`, `READ_OBJECTIVE`,
  `REQUIREMENTS`, `READ_FINDINGS`, `READ_ARCHIVE`, `READ_TOOL_OUTPUT`, MCP, plugins. `HARNESS_TOOLS`, `KNOWN_TOOLS` and the serve-mcp list
  are derived from the registry's baseline set, so they are identical.
- **One execution path:** `ExecutionSpine.execute` resolves the handler only through `registry.resolve(name).binding`. The fallback chain at
  `spine.ts:566-569` and the `context.defaultHandler` and bridge fallbacks are removed **only after** the slice-1 table proves equivalence.
  Pipeline stages named as the unit asks: **approve** (dispatch decide/confirm), **sandbox** (unchanged, inside `bridge.executeTool` for
  `bridge` bindings), **run** (`spine.execute`), **hooks** (`pluginManager.notifyToolCall` before execution,
  `notifyToolResult`/`executeToolPipeline` after; HK-1 attaches here later).
- **Dispatch decomposition** (behaviour-preserving, side-effect order preserved), in new `cli/src/core/tool_pipeline.ts`:
  - `parseToolArguments(call)` → `{args, structurallyRepaired}`;
  - `admitToolCall(agent, name, args, ...)` → `{refuse: receipt} | {ok}` for phases 2-3;
  - `decideToolCall(agent, ...)` → `{refuse} | {ask: question} | {run}` for phase 4;
  - `confirmToolCall(...)` for phase 5;
  - `executeToolCall(...)` for phase 6;
  - `afterToolCall(...)` for phase 7.

  **`dispatchToolCallImpl` stays in `core/dispatch_tool_call.ts` under the same name and signature** as a straight-line orchestrator
  (target CC ≤ 20, nesting ≤ 2). The baseline then measures a much smaller function against 288/6 and passes.
- **Baseline handling (D-MT2-2):** do not edit `critical-complexity-baseline.json` during slices 2-3. The extracted functions are new and
  untracked. Slice 4 is one small PR, made after the last extraction merges. It:
  - moves `baselineRevision` to that merge commit (an ancestor of HEAD);
  - adds `decideToolCall`, `admitToolCall`, `confirmToolCall`, `executeToolCall` and `afterToolCall` (`file: cli/src/core/tool_pipeline.ts`)
    to `functions`;
  - updates `critical_complexity.test.ts` (revision; `rows.length` 5 → 10);
  - pastes the checker's before/after table into the PR.

  This is tighten-only: the gate had already proved every tracked function ≤ the old baseline, so advancing can only lower the
  references. It changes the gate's reference commit, so it lands only with the owner's acknowledgement (merge role per memory). If
  declined, the extracted functions stay untracked and `dispatchToolCallImpl` keeps its new low numbers against the old reference.
- **No new grant path:**
  - the registry has no API that lowers an effect, marks a tool approval-free or overrides `requiresDecision`;
  - an extension cannot register `read_workspace` or `internal`;
  - `decideToolCall` is the only function returning `{run}` for an asking effect, and only after `confirm` or an operator rule exactly as
    today;
  - allow-always remains the sidecar's or REPL's concern, untouched.

### Security analysis
The risk is a silent behaviour change in a gate during the move. Mitigations:
- characterization tables land first and stay byte-identical;
- each extraction PR moves one phase group;
- no phase changes order;
- refusal receipts keep their exact text and `status`;
- the G-3 focused set (below) runs on every slice at head and at base (`review-run-existing-suites` lesson);
- registry construction **fails closed** at startup (a spec without a binding throws), which differs from opencode's skip-and-log
  (`packages/core/src/tool.ts:246`), rejected.

### Files
Add: `cli/src/core/tool_registry.ts`, `cli/src/core/tool_pipeline.ts`, `cli/test/tool_surface_characterization.test.ts`,
`cli/test/tool_dispatch_characterization.test.ts`, `cli/test/mt1_core_import.test.ts`, `cli/test/tool_registry.test.ts`,
`cli/test/fixtures/model_tools_v1.json`, `cli/test/fixtures/tool_bindings_v1.json`, `docs/TOOL_REGISTRY.md` (how to add a tool).
Change: `cli/src/core/capabilities.ts`, `cli/src/core/spine.ts`, `cli/src/core/spine_handlers.ts`, `cli/src/tools.ts`
(`registerBridgeCapabilities`), `cli/src/agent.ts` (`effectiveTools`, registration), `cli/src/core/dispatch_tool_call.ts`,
`cli/src/parser.ts`, `cli/src/mcp.ts` (derived lists), and in slice 4 `cli/critical-complexity-baseline.json` and
`cli/test/critical_complexity.test.ts`.

### Tests
**Characterization, before any refactor (slice 1); green before and after every later slice; fixtures regenerate only with
`NEXUS_TOOLS_RECORD=1`, and a diff needs review:**
1. `tool_surface_characterization`: `getEffectiveTools()` for a matrix covering:
   - role (main + every `AgentRole`), depth 0/1;
   - objective present/absent, skills present/absent, mask on/off;
   - groups none / one / all;
   - a delegated allow-list;
   - one fake MCP tool and one plugin tool.

   It records names in order plus the SHA-256 and byte length of `JSON.stringify(tools)` into `model_tools_v1.json`. Also `HARNESS_TOOLS`
   bytes, `KNOWN_TOOLS`, serve-mcp `tools/list` and the ACP kind table.
2. `tool_dispatch_characterization`: for every registered name, record which source resolves (spine handler / registry handler /
   capability.handler / defaultHandler / bridge), `effect`, `mutating`, `changesWorkspace` → `tool_bindings_v1.json`.
3. Same file: the **decision matrix** from `dispatchToolCall` with a counting `onConfirm` and a stub bridge. Rows are a representative tool
   per effect class, `run_command` with a CS-9 allow/prompt/forbidden rule, a managed `require_human`, and a verification-path write.
   Columns are modes review/auto/read-only × fullAccess. It records ask / deny / run and the refusal text.
4. Same file: **side-effect order** for one write and one `run_command`: the sequence of observer, plugin, flight, journal and
   `logAudit` calls.
5. `mt1_core_import`: a child process imports `src/core/app.ts` with argv `--help run`: exit 0, empty stdout, no commander help, no file
   under a fresh HOME (MT-1's missing acceptance test).

**New behaviour (slice 2):** `tool_registry.test.ts`:
- duplicate names, a missing binding, `spec.handler` plus a binding, and an extension with `read_workspace` effect are each refused at
  construction;
- **adding a tool = one `register({spec, binding, offer})`** makes it visible in `modelTools` and dispatchable, with no other file edited (a
  test-only tool);
- no exported API changes an effect after registration.

**Focused suites run on every slice:** `command_rules_dispatch`, `managed_policy_dispatch`, `vllm_nullable_dispatch`, `approval_policy`,
`injection_gate`, `security_gates`, `sandbox_denial_events`, `role_deny_lists`, `tool_groups`, `capabilities`, `lsp_shape`,
`acp_mapping`, `acp_stdio`, `sidecar`, `subagent_delegation_authority`, `agt111_subagent_parity`, `verify_hostile`, `context_convergence`,
`critical_complexity`, and `check_critical_complexity.ts` output in the PR.

### Slices
1. **S/M:** tests 1-5 and fixtures only. Safe any time; touches no source.
2. **M:** `tool_registry.ts`; `capabilities.ts`, `spine.ts`, `spine_handlers.ts`, `tools.ts`, `agent.ts` (`effectiveTools`), `parser.ts`,
   `mcp.ts`. Characterization stays identical. Hot: `agent.ts`, `spine_handlers.ts` (claimed now).
3. **L, as 3 PRs** in this order, each with `dispatchToolCallImpl` CC strictly lower:
   - 3a `afterToolCall` + `executeToolCall`;
   - 3b `admitToolCall` + `parseToolArguments`;
   - 3c `decideToolCall` + `confirmToolCall`.

   Hot: `dispatch_tool_call.ts`.
4. **S:** baseline advance (D-MT2-2), owner-acknowledged.

**When it is safest:** last of the five units, after the Codex lanes on `agent.ts`, `spine_handlers.ts`, `run_turn.ts`, `agent_support.ts`
and `objective.ts` release (context-maturity, WP-P10-02, PA-3/PA-4). Also after SB-1 slice 3 and PF-3 have touched dispatch and the sidecar,
and with a short, announced claim freeze on `dispatch_tool_call.ts`, `spine*.ts` and `capabilities.ts` during slice 3. Slice 1 can land
immediately and protects everyone else's work too.

Out of scope: moving the sandbox into dispatch; parallel tool batches (Codex orchestrator); HK-1 hooks themselves; `runTurnImpl`;
splitting the TUI files.

on failure".

export type RouteSource = "spine-handler" | "registry-handler" | "mcp" | "plugin" | "pipeline-bridge";

/**
 * Which of today's handler sources `ExecutionSpine.execute` resolves for a registered tool, in its order: the spine's
 * own handler map, then the registry's handler (the same object as `capability.handler`), then the default handler
 * dispatch builds (MCP, plugin tool, else the plugin pipeline around the bridge).
 */
export function routeProbe(agent: AutonomousAgent, name: string): RouteSource {
  const a = agent as any;
  if (agent.getSpine().getHandler(name)) return "spine-handler";
  if (agent.getCapabilityRegistry().getHandler(name)) return "registry-handler";
  if (a.mcpManager.isMcpTool(name)) return "mcp";
  if (a.pluginManager.isCustomTool(name)) return "plugin";
  return "pipeline-bridge";
}
